event.title: The Aral Sea was drained, the dust still blows
event.summary: From the 1960s, Soviet irrigation diverted the Amu Darya and Syr Darya. The Aral Sea lost most of its water, exposing a poisoned seabed, the Aralkum, that still launches salt-and-pesticide dust across Central Asia. UNEP and UNCCD documents show people are still breathing that legacy.
event.hero: They turned a sea into a desert that still storms our lungs.

nodes.title: Rivers were diverted to grow cotton
nodes.description: From the 1960s, Soviet irrigation diverted the Amu Darya and Syr Darya into upstream cotton and farm canals. Those rivers had been the Aral Sea’s inflow. Mass diversion starved the sea of water on purpose, as a development plan, not as an accident.

nodes.title: The sea emptied and salinity exploded
nodes.description: The Aral lost most of its volume and area. Fisheries collapsed. The sea’s old climate-buffering role went with the water. What remained was a much smaller, saltier remnant and a growing dry bed.

nodes.title: A new desert of toxic dust was born
nodes.description: The dry lakebed became the Aralkum, a source of salt- and pollutant-laden dust storms. Pesticides and salts that had settled in the seabed were left on the surface. Wind turned that residue into a regional air problem.

nodes.title: Dust still breaches WHO air thresholds
nodes.description: Models show Aralkum dust alone can push Nukus over WHO daily PM10 limits dozens of days a year. The desert still storms. People downwind still breathe what used to sit under a sea.

nodes.title: Respiratory and chronic illness remain elevated
nodes.description: UNCCD cites millions affected and disease rates far above national averages. Dust is not the only cause. Poverty, pesticides, and health-system gaps also matter, and the sources say so.

nodes.title: Livelihoods and towns emptied
nodes.description: When the fisheries died, towns built on the water lost their work. UNCCD notes displacement of more than 100,000 people. Empty harbours are part of the record, not a metaphor.

nodes.title: Salt fallout still cuts farm productivity
nodes.description: Uzbek assessments cited by UNCCD find atmospheric salt fallout cuts farmland bioproductivity about 5–10% and pastures 20–30%. The dust does not only enter lungs. It lands on fields.

nodes.title: 2025: UNEP still warns of Aral-origin dust
nodes.description: A UNEP Uzbekistan sand and dust storm report traced an extreme pollution spike to a plume from the Aral region about 900 km away. The 1960s diversion is still an air-quality event in the 2020s.

nodes.title: Recovery is generational, not finished
nodes.description: Partial North Aral restoration exists. South Aral and Aralkum dust, and the health burdens that come with them, persist. Recovery here is measured in generations, not in a single project year.

claims.text: From the 1960s, over-exploitation of the Amu Darya and Syr Darya for irrigation caused the Aral Sea to lose ~80% of its volume and shrink to about a third of its former area.
The exposed seabed became a major dust source (Aralkum), with documented increases in local dust-storm activity.
Regional modelling (2024): Aralkum dust alone can exceed WHO daily PM10 (45 µg/m³) on ~29 days/year in Nukus, ~8 in Bukhara, ~2 in Tashkent.
claims.caveat: Modelled Aralkum-only dust; other deserts also contribute.

claims.text: UNCCD Central Asia SDS strategy: Aral disaster affected health of over 5 million people region-wide; disease rates in Aral districts reported far above national averages, peer-reviewed reviews caution dust is not the sole cause.
claims.caveat: Multi-causal: pesticides, poverty, and dust intertwine.

claims.text: UNCCD strategy: environmental disaster of the Aral Sea region led to displacement of more than 100,000 people.
UNCCD citing Uzbek hydromet: salt fallout reduces farmland bioproductivity by 5–10% and pastures by 20–30%.
UNEP (16 Dec 2025): sand and dust storms drive Uzbekistan’s worst urban air spikes; the highest daily PM spike in Termez was traced to a dust plume originating from the Aral Sea region ~900 km away.
Partial North Aral recovery exists, but South Aral dust, SDS risk, and health inequities remain active into the 2020s, a multi-generation ripple.
claims.caveat: Depends on restoration funding and climate.

predictions.title: Nukus still faces ~month/year of WHO-breaching Aralkum dust days
predictions.method: Use published model count (29 days exceeding WHO daily PM10 from Aralkum dust) as verified exposure-frequency bound.
verified_against: E3S 2024 Aralkum dust modelling vs WHO PM10
predictions.caveat: Single-model year; other dust sources add days.

timeline.label: Diversion begins
timeline.detail: Irrigation expansions cut river inflow; sea level starts falling.

timeline.label: Sea collapse
timeline.detail: Volume loss ~80%; fisheries collapse; Aralkum expands.

timeline.label: Dust still travels hundreds of km
timeline.detail: UNEP 2025: Aral-region plume hits Termez ~900 km away.

timeline.label: Generational recovery
timeline.detail: SDS strategies run through 2030; health burdens lag physical restoration.

what_we_know: Irrigation diversion collapsed the Aral Sea.
The dry bed still emits dust that can breach WHO air guidelines.
UN institutions still treat Aral-linked sand and dust storms as an active regional health threat in the 2020s.
what_remains_uncertain: The exact fraction of disease burden attributable to dust versus pesticides and poverty.
How fast South Aral dust emissions will fall under current restoration plans.
